caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Serbia's debt peaked at 67.1% of GDP in 2015 on the post-crisis adjustment and state-enterprise losses, then fell steadily to a projected 42.4% in 2025 (54.3% in 2020, 50.9% in 2022), one of the region's best consolidations. It was 37% in 2006 (29.4% in 2008, the low). GDP tripled from $33.4bn in 2006 to a projected $100.0bn in 2025. IMF programs anchored the 2014-18 fiscal adjustment — subsidy cuts, public-sector wage restraint — and the results have held. Debt sustainability is comfortable; the fiscal question is investment execution, not solvency.
inflation_management: The National Bank of Serbia targets 3% (+/-1.5pp), and the record shows steady improvement: 12.4% in 2008 (the series high) on the pre-crisis boom, 8.1% in 2009, then single digits through the 2010s, bottoming at 1.1% in 2016. It was 1.5% in 2020, rose to 12% in 2022 on the energy shock, then fell to 4.7% in 2024 and a projected 3.9% for 2025 — near the top of the tolerance band. The managed-float dinar has been kept broadly stable, which helped anchor expectations; the NBS has built credibility over the decade.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis ended the pre-crisis boom; IMF standby arrangement (2009) stabilized the dinar.
Debt peaked at 67.1% of GDP; the 2014 IMF program began the fiscal consolidation.
Inflation bottomed at 1.1% as the consolidation and stable dinar anchored expectations.
COVID-19: debt rose to 54.3% of GDP; the fiscal response was sizable but temporary.
Energy shock inflation of 12%; EXPO 2027 preparations drove a public-investment push.

outlook_next_decade: Serbia's outlook balances strong macro management against political risk: debt falling toward 42% of GDP, inflation near target, and the EXPO 2027 investment cycle supporting growth. EU accession talks continue but slowly; the Kosovo dispute remains the geopolitical overhang. The growth model — FDI in manufacturing, IT services — is working. Risks are political instability, which flared in 2024-25, and energy dependence. The analytical base case is continued convergence with inflation at target.
